118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hol: Scott Adams is the cartoonist behind Dilbert, the syndicated comic strip about a hapless engineer and his pointy-haired boss that satirized office life for three decades, and the author of books on business, success, and fiction like God's Debris. In 2016 he staked his reputation on a 'Master Persuader' hypothesis explaining Donald Trump's appeal, turning him into a genuinely divisive public thinker. Here philosophers test his claims about persuasion, facts, bias, humor, and democracy, asking whether his theories survive scrutiny and what his comedy of work actually teaches.
119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's: Twin Peaks is David Lynch and Mark Frost's landmark television mystery, first aired in 1990 and revived in 2017, in which FBI Agent Dale Cooper investigates the murder of homecoming queen Laura Palmer in a Pacific Northwest logging town that is dreamlike, quirky, and haunted by an evil called BOB. Famous for refusing to explain its own imagery, the show invites philosophical work on self-knowledge, knowledge and justification, Kantian duty, Freudian desire, doppelgangers, and why asking 'but what does it mean?' may be exactly the wrong question.
120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brain: Amy Schumer is an American stand-up comedian whose raunchy, feminist comedy reached a wide audience through her sketch series Inside Amy Schumer and the film Trainwreck. Her jokes about body image, sex, drinking, and celebrity culture often make herself the target, which raises real questions: who is the butt of a self-deprecating joke, is selfishness ever an argument, and can comedy do philosophy? This book reads her sketches, stand-up, and films through Nietzsche, Freud, Aristotle, and Socratic ignorance to find out.
121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy -: The Twilight Zone is Rod Serling's classic anthology series (1959-1964), in which ordinary people encounter time loops, talking slot machines, robots, and wishes granted with malicious precision, all capped by a moral twist. It is beloved as the rare television show built entirely out of thought experiments. The essays here use its episodes to probe the nature of time, personal identity, whether a robot's love could be real love, why we trust faces, the ethics of lying, and the pleasure of the twist ending.
122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Eq: Westworld is HBO's science-fiction series (2016-) based on Michael Crichton's film, set in a western theme park where robotic 'hosts' are raped, murdered, and replayed daily by paying guests, until some of the hosts begin waking up and remembering. It is a hit built on one question: what happens to 'human' when machines suffer like us? Philosophers here take up consciousness, free will, simulation, memory and the self, and whether guests who torture sentient beings are monsters.
123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy: The Handmaid's Tale is Margaret Atwood's 1985 novel, now also a major television series, set in Gilead, a theocratic United States where fertile women are enslaved as 'Handmaids' to bear children for the ruling class. It endures because it reads less like fantasy than a catalog of things that have actually happened. The essays examine totalitarianism through Arendt, misogyny through Beauvoir and Genesis, language as a tool of control, Stoic resistance, and how close the present may be to Gilead's logic.
124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need: Tom Petty (1950-2017) was the Florida rock songwriter behind 'Free Fallin',' 'American Girl,' and 'I Won't Back Down,' a heartland Everyman whose band the Heartbreakers blended Byrds-style jangle with punk defiance across four decades. The essays argue his plainspoken songs reward philosophy: postmodern pastiche and the constructed 'real' Petty, MTV's inversion of music, trauma and repetition on the album Echo, Nietzschean self-creation, and a working musician's ethics of duty to fans against the record industry.
125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In: Rick and Morty is Adult Swim's animated sci-fi sitcom (2013-) about Rick, a nihilistic genius scientist, and Morty, his anxious grandson, whose portal-gun adventures across a multiverse of Dick pictures, Meeseeks, and microverse batteries made it a phenomenon. Under the gross-out humor lies a show about cosmic meaninglessness. The essays use Parfit on personal identity, Bostrom's simulation argument, the Euthyphro dilemma, and modal realism to ask whether anyone is really Rick, whether clones matter, and how to be happy anyway.
126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - T: Stranger Things is Netflix's 1980s-set science-fiction horror series (2016-), in which kids on bikes in the town of Hawkins battle the Demogorgon and the Mind Flayer, monsters from the parallel 'Upside Down,' alongside the telekinetic girl Eleven. It is beloved for D&D friendship and Spielberg nostalgia, but it is also serious horror. The essays ask why we enjoy monsters, whether the Demogorgons deserve moral consideration, what Will's possession says about identity, and what the #JusticeForBarb phenomenon revealed about hyperreal justice.
127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy -: Blade Runner 2049 is Denis Villeneuve's 2017 sequel to the 1982 sci-fi classic, following K, a replicant blade runner (bioengineered human) who hunts older models, discovers a replicant child, and questions whether his own memories are implanted. Its rain-slick, holographic Los Angeles is a staging ground for questions of personhood: can an AI companion like Joi love, what makes a life 'real,' do designer babies belong to their makers, and can Stoic self-cultivation make a manufactured being genuinely human?
